name: Australia
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Capital gains tax at marginal rates up to 45%, halved by the 50% discount for assets held over 12 months (Coincub CTR 2025; ATO).
banking: Banks are wary of crypto, so moving money in and out can be difficult. Australia's banks are wary of crypto. Commonwealth Bank, the largest, caps payments to crypto exchanges at AUD 10,000 a month and can hold or decline transfers for 24 hours. Its subsidiary Bankwest applies similar limits. Bank of Queensland caps crypto payments at AUD 5,000 a month, HSBC blocks payments to crypto exchanges altogether, and Macquarie customers often report declined transfers. NAB and Westpac block payments to exchanges they consider 'high-risk'. ANZ, ING and several smaller banks are more workable, but extra fraud checks on larger transfers are common (The Block; Blockworks; Digital Surge banking guide 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. First comprehensive digital asset law passed in 2026 (Digital Asset Platforms and Tokenised Custody Platforms under the Corporations Act). Travel Rule obligations live from 1 July 2026 (Contentworks; Elliptic).
residency: Moving here is very difficult, or needs a very large investment. One of the hardest OECD countries to immigrate to. Points-based, slow, expensive. No crypto-friendly residency path.
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. About 172 listed merchants (coinpedia).
community: There is an active bitcoin community with meetups and events. Ranked 15th of 117 countries for everyday crypto use in Chainalysis's 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index. Local scene: Strong meetup, developer, and startup ecosystem in major cities. Attitudes: Neutral but compliance-oriented culture.
privacy: Limited privacy: crypto activity is reported to the tax office and shared with other countries soon. Australia closely tracks crypto. Every exchange must register with AUSTRAC, the financial-intelligence agency, and the tax office (ATO) runs a data-matching programme that has requested names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, email and social-media accounts, bank details, wallet addresses and full transaction histories for up to 1.2 million accounts covering July 2023 to June 2026. Australia will also share crypto account data with other countries under the international crypto tax-reporting agreement (CARF) from 2028 (ATO via Koinly and Crypto Tax Calculator; OECD June 2026).
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: 5 out of 5 (World Justice Project 2025 score 0.80, ranked 11 of 143 countries). Currency: 4 out of 5 (hard peg, euro or a stable major currency). Risk of a sudden change in crypto rules: 5 out of 5. Peace and security: 4 out of 5 (Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.602, ranked 20 of 163 countries).
summary: Ranked 134th out of 249 countries (mixed). Best for stability (5 out of 5). Weakest area is residency (1 out of 5).

banking: Most banks let you move money to and from crypto platforms without much trouble. EU transfer rules require providers to collect data on transfers to and from self-hosted wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).

Settlement permit for financially independent people (Niederlassungsbewilligung – ausgenommen Erwerbstätigkeit): about EUR 2,548 a month, German language required, annual quota of roughly 450 places (oesterreich.gv.at 2026; Nomad Watch; VigoLex).

name: El Salvador

privacy: Georgia has not signed up to the international system for sharing crypto account information between tax offices, so your crypto data is not automatically shared abroad.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks Georgia's rule of law 52nd out of 143 countries. The local currency, the lari, can lose value, and the country has been in a political crisis since 2024, though there have been no moves against crypto. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 93rd of 163 countries (3 out of 5).
summary: Ranked 4th out of 249 countries. Georgia combines no tax on crypto profits, a year of visa-free living for many nationalities and strong privacy. The main risks are a volatile currency and political uncertainty.

spending: Berlin and other cities have bitcoin-accepting businesses, and Germany is among the leading countries for listed merchants, but paying in bitcoin is not yet mainstream.

name: Panama
tax: Panama only taxes money earned inside the country. Because selling bitcoin on a foreign exchange counts as foreign income, residents pay nothing on those gains. There is no minimum holding period, no wealth tax on your bitcoin, and no need to report foreign income to the tax office.
banking: Banking is one of Panama's biggest strengths. Towerbank has openly welcomed bitcoin users since 2022: it accepts money coming from exchanges, issues a debit card, runs a platform that holds bitcoin and dollars side by side, and has made more than $10 million of bitcoin-backed loans. The state-owned Caja de Ahorros is designing bitcoin accounts of its own.
legal: Nothing in Panamanian law stops you from buying, holding, storing, sending or paying with bitcoin, and you need no licence to do any of it. A 2022 crypto law was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2023. The new bills now being discussed are aimed at crypto businesses, not at individuals.
residency: Panama has some of the easiest residency routes in the world. Retirees can qualify with a pension of about $1,000 a month. Citizens of around 50 'friendly nations' can qualify with a local job or about $200,000 in property or savings. Investors can get permanent residency in roughly 30 to 45 business days by buying $300,000 of property, a figure expected to rise after 15 October 2026.
spending: Panama City lets people pay taxes, fees, fines, permits and even bus tickets in bitcoin, with a partner bank converting the payment into dollars straight away. Some property developers and agencies also accept crypto, although many prefer dollar-backed stablecoins. Shops that take bitcoin exist, but they are not yet found everywhere.
community: Panama City's mayor, Mayer Mizrachi, is one of the most outspoken supporters of bitcoin in the region. He introduced the city's crypto payments and has even suggested priority Canal passage for ships that pay in bitcoin. Bitcoin Day Panama brings banks, regulators and enthusiasts together each year, and local groups run regular meetups.
privacy: Panama has agreed to join the international system for sharing crypto account information between tax offices, starting in 2028. It already shares bank account information with other countries, and banks carry out thorough identity checks. On the plus side, there is no wealth tax and no requirement to declare income earned abroad.
stability: Panama has used the US dollar since 1904, so there is no risk of the local currency losing value. It has a long record of peaceful elections, and S&P confirmed its investment-grade rating in September 2026. The weak spot is the court system, which the World Justice Project ranks 73rd out of 143 countries. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 80th of 163 countries (3 out of 5).
summary: Ranked 1st out of 249 countries. Panama comes top because it scores highly almost everywhere: no tax on foreign bitcoin gains, banks that openly serve bitcoin users, complete legal freedom and some of the easiest residency rules in the world. Its only middling score is privacy, as it will start sharing crypto account data with other countries in 2028.

name: Philippines
tax: The Philippines charges a 15% tax on gains from selling crypto. Mining and staking are taxed as income, and VAT can apply to crypto payments.
banking: Buying bitcoin is easy. UnionBank, one of the country's biggest banks, lets customers buy and sell crypto in its app. GCash, with about 90 million accounts, and Maya also offer crypto inside their apps.
legal: Crypto is legal and licensed, but rules tightened in July 2025: platforms serving Filipinos must be local companies. The regulator named ten unregistered overseas exchanges, including OKX, Bybit and Kraken, and they can no longer be funded through GCash.
residency: The Philippines has one of Asia's easiest retirement visas, requiring a pension of about $800 a month plus a $10,000 deposit (from age 40). There is also a digital nomad visa for those earning about $2,000 a month.
spending: Some businesses accept bitcoin, but crypto use is mostly about trading rather than shopping.
community: The Philippines ranks 19th in the world for everyday crypto use in Chainalysis's 2026 index, with a very strong trading community and positive attitudes to crypto.
privacy: The Philippines will start sharing crypto account information with other countries' tax offices in 2028.
stability: The World Justice Project ranks the country's rule of law 97th out of 143 countries, and the peso is a moderately stable floating currency. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 101st of 163 countries (3 out of 5).
summary: Ranked 26th out of 249 countries. The Philippines stands out for very easy bank access to bitcoin and one of Asia's most affordable retirement visas. Tighter platform rules and a 15% tax are the downsides.

name: Poland

banking: Most banks let you move money to and from crypto platforms without much trouble. EU residents can use banks that sell crypto in-app across the bloc – Revolut (MiCA licence via Cyprus, Lithuanian bank licence), N26, bunq – and transfer to EU-licensed exchanges over SEPA. Local bank appetite varies and large transfers draw anti-money-laundering reviews (cryptocardtools 2026; changenow).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) fully applicable since 30 December 2024. National transitional periods for existing providers ended by 1 July 2026. Individuals are free to hold, store in their own wallets and trade. EU transfer rules require providers to collect data on transfers to and from self-hosted wallets (FMA Liechtenstein; Börse Express Jul 2026).
residency: Moving here is possible, but you will need a good income or savings. Residency moderate (EU easier; non-EU standard).

privacy: Limited privacy: crypto activity is reported to the tax office and shared with other countries soon. Under EU rules (DAC8), crypto platforms report customer activity to tax offices from 2026, and EU countries begin sharing this data with each other in 2027.

name: Portugal
tax: Since 2023, gains on crypto held for more than a year are tax-free for individuals in Portugal. Gains on crypto held for less than a year are taxed at a flat 28%, and staking or professional trading falls under normal income tax.
banking: Portugal uses the EU's standard bank-transfer system. Banks generally accept money coming from regulated exchanges if you can show the paperwork, although some banks are more welcoming than others.
legal: The EU's crypto rules apply. Individuals are free to hold and use bitcoin, but platforms must record details of transfers to and from personal wallets.
residency: Portugal's passive-income (D7) visa and digital nomad visa are open to people with a modest monthly income, and a 'golden visa' is still available through investment funds.
spending: Lisbon and Madeira have visible clusters of businesses that accept bitcoin, supported by a large community of people who have moved there.
community: Portugal has one of Europe's largest communities of bitcoiners who have relocated there, with frequent meetups and conferences and a lively digital-nomad scene.
privacy: Under EU rules, crypto platforms have had to collect customer information since 2026, and EU tax offices start sharing it with each other in 2027.
stability: Portugal uses the euro and the World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 29th out of 143 countries. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 7th of 163 countries (5 out of 5).
summary: Ranked 7th out of 249 countries. Portugal pairs tax-free long-term bitcoin gains with accessible visas, a large international bitcoin community and EU stability. The main drawback is EU-wide reporting of crypto activity.

name: Puerto Rico
tax: US citizens who genuinely move to Puerto Rico can pay 0% local tax on capital gains made after the move, if they apply for the Act 60 tax decree by 31 December 2026. From 2027, new applicants are set to pay 4%, subject to final approval. Only US citizens benefit, and there are yearly donation and property requirements.
banking: Puerto Rico uses the US banking system, with full access to US exchanges, bitcoin funds and storage providers, under strict US rules.
legal: US federal law applies, and individuals are free to hold and use bitcoin.
residency: Puerto Rico is open to US citizens without any visa. People from other countries need US immigration status, which is hard to get.
spending: San Juan has a cluster of bitcoin-accepting businesses, helped by the many bitcoiners who have moved there.
community: Puerto Rico has a large community of bitcoiners who have relocated there and hosts frequent events.
privacy: US federal reporting rules apply, so crypto brokers report your trades to the US tax office.
stability: Puerto Rico operates within the US legal system and uses the US dollar. The Global Peace Index does not cover it, so its stability score is based on the other three measures.
summary: Ranked 21st out of 249 countries. For US citizens, Puerto Rico is a unique option: 0% local tax on new gains (for decrees applied for in 2026), US banking and a big bitcoin community. For everyone else, residency is difficult.

Crypto businesses, and many crypto payments, have to go through licensed providers.
residency: Getting residency is relatively easy. A two-year visa comes with property worth about $204,000, the ten-year Golden Visa with property of about $545,000, and there are also remote-work, freelancer and company-based visas.
spending: Around 120 businesses in the UAE publicly accept bitcoin, mostly in Dubai. Luxury shops, some hotels and many property developers take crypto through licensed payment companies, and Dubai has trialled government payments in crypto, converted into dirhams.
community: Dubai and Abu Dhabi host some of the world's biggest crypto conferences and are home to thousands of crypto companies. The scene is mostly professional and business-focused, with a smaller grassroots bitcoin culture than places like El Salvador or Switzerland.
privacy: The UAE will start sharing crypto account information with other countries' tax offices in 2028, and it already shares bank account data. Identity checks are strict. Because there is no personal income tax, there is no annual tax return to file.
stability: The dirham has been tied to the US dollar for decades and the country is politically very stable. The World Justice Project ranks its rule of law 37th out of 143 countries, and the UAE was removed from the international money-laundering 'grey list' in 2024. On peace and security, the Global Peace Index 2026 ranks it 72nd of 163 countries (3 out of 5).
summary: Ranked 2nd out of 249 countries. The UAE is a top choice for people who want zero tax, easy residency and a big professional crypto scene. Everyday spending in bitcoin is still limited, and crypto account data will be shared internationally from 2028.

name: United Kingdom
tax: Bitcoin gains are taxed at a fairly high rate. Capital gains tax at 18%/24% for 2025/26 with a GBP 3,000 annual allowance (Coincub CTR 2025).
banking: Banks are wary of crypto, so moving money in and out can be difficult. UK banks are among the most restrictive in Europe. Nine major banks limit or block payments to crypto exchanges, and industry research says about 40% of bank-to-exchange transfers are blocked or delayed. Chase UK, Starling, TSB, Metro Bank and Virgin Money block crypto payments entirely. HSBC and Barclays cap them at £2,500 per payment and £10,000 per 30 days, NatWest at £1,000 a day and £5,000 a month, Santander at £1,000 per payment and £3,000 a month, and Nationwide at £5,000 a day. Lloyds (including Halifax and Bank of Scotland), Revolut and Monzo (within a £5,000 rolling limit) are the more workable options, and money coming back from exchanges is generally accepted (crypto.news; CoinDesk Jan 2026; Datawallet Jul 2026).
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. Cryptoassets Regulations passed 4 February 2026. FCA final rules published 30 June 2026. Full licensing regime starts 25 October 2027 (A&O Shearman; KPMG; IG). Individuals free.
residency: Moving here is difficult or expensive. No dedicated digital nomad visa (Ellis Immigration, 2026). Residence mainly via work, study, family or investment routes. In practice: Residency: hard (work or family routes; high cost)
spending: Some places accept bitcoin, mostly in bigger cities. About 451 listed bitcoin merchants (coinpedia).
community: There is an active bitcoin community with meetups and events. Ranked 17th of 117 countries for everyday crypto use in Chainalysis's 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index. Local scene: Large developer or finance crypto community and active meetup scenes. Attitudes: Positive and mainstream investor sentiment, though regulatory caution exists.
privacy: Limited privacy: crypto activity is reported to the tax office and shared with other countries soon. This country has signed up to the international crypto tax-reporting agreement (CARF), so crypto platforms' customer data will be shared automatically with other countries' tax offices from 2027.
stability: Very stable: strong rule of law, a strong currency and little risk of sudden rule changes. Rule of law: 5 out of 5 (World Justice Project 2025 score 0.78, ranked 14 of 143 countries). Currency: 4 out of 5 (hard peg, euro or a stable major currency). Risk of a sudden change in crypto rules: 5 out of 5. Peace and security: 4 out of 5 (Global Peace Index 2026 score 1.730, ranked 39 of 163 countries).
summary: Ranked 120th out of 249 countries (mixed). Best for stability (5 out of 5). Weakest areas are tax, banking, residency and privacy (2 out of 5).

name: United States
tax: Bitcoin is heavily taxed here, or the tax rules are harsh. The IRS treats bitcoin as property, so every sale, swap or purchase with bitcoin is a taxable event with no small-amount exemption. Long-term gains are taxed at 0, 15 or 20% federally plus state tax, and short-term gains at ordinary rates. US citizens are taxed on worldwide income wherever they live.
banking: Banks openly work with bitcoin users, so buying and selling through your bank is easy. The US has the deepest bitcoin financial market in the world, including bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), major exchanges and custodians, with heavy compliance requirements.
legal: Bitcoin is legal and clearly regulated, and individuals are free to use it. Bitcoin is legal. The GENIUS Act (2025) regulates stablecoins, a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve was created by executive order, and the CLARITY Act on market structure is still pending in the Senate.
residency: Moving here is difficult or expensive. Residency is immigration-based and hard to obtain.
spending: A good number of businesses accept bitcoin. The US has the highest absolute number of bitcoin-accepting merchants in the world.
community: There is a large, lively bitcoin community with regular events. The largest bitcoin community in the world, with major conferences, developers and companies.
privacy: Very little privacy: crypto activity is closely tracked, reported or restricted. Brokers report transactions on Form 1099-DA, and US citizens must also report foreign bank accounts to the authorities (FBAR and FATCA rules).
stability: Fairly stable, with some risks to keep in mind. The World Justice Project Rule of Law Index 2025 scores the US 0.68 (rank 27). Peace and security: the Global Peace Index 2026 scores United States 2.535 (rank 133 of 163), which counts as 1 out of 5 in our stability score.
summary: Ranked 98th out of 249 countries (good). Best for banking and community (5 out of 5). Weakest areas are tax and privacy (1 out of 5).
